name: Pan-Islamism
summary: Pan-Islamism calls for the political unity and solidarity of Muslims on the basis of religion rather than ethnicity or territorial nation, and for joint resistance to European domination. It arose in the late 19th century around Abdulhamid II's caliphate and Afghani and Abduh's writings, was carried on by Rida and the interwar Muslim congresses, and survives in the state-level Organisation of Islamic Cooperation and the caliphate-state programme of Hizb ut-Tahrir.
scope: Only its position on the national question: unity of the Muslim community, nation and territory, foreign domination, kin abroad, minorities and the means it accepts. Based on Afghani and Abduh (al-Urwa al-Wuthqa, 1884) and Rida's caliphate writings as reported by Hourani, Abdulhamid II's policy and the Muslim congresses of 1926-35 as reported by Kramer, the OIC charter and, for the single-state strand, the Hizb ut-Tahrir draft constitution. The economic and social programmes of Islamist parties, Shia revolutionary Islam and jihadist movements are not used.

keyFigures.name: Jamal al-Din al-Afghani
keyFigures.role: Early advocate of Muslim unity against European imperialism, co-editor of al-Urwa al-Wuthqa.

keyFigures.name: Rashid Rida
keyFigures.role: Reformer who tied Muslim unity to a caliphate that applies the Sharia and promoted Muslim congresses.

keyFigures.name: Abdul Hamid II
keyFigures.role: Ottoman sultan-caliph whose policy made Muslim solidarity around his caliphate a state aim.

missingStatements.text: States that share a religion should coordinate a unified position in international forums.
missingStatements.rationale: The OIC charter makes promoting a unified position on issues of common interest in international fora an objective, and the congresses aimed at common Muslim action.

notes: Pan-Islamism is a unifying aim more than a programme, so most statements are null. Strands differ on form: Abdulhamid's absolute sultan-caliph, Afghani's cooperation of Muslim rulers without a single state (Hourani: no sign he meant one), Rida's caliphate of necessity, the OIC's sovereign member states, and Hizb ut-Tahrir's single state; Iqbal denied any political Pan-Islamism. Themes searched: unity, nation and territory, foreign domination and colonialism, caliphate and government, jihad and violence, Palestine, minorities, sovereignty and international bodies, religion and law. Rida's own Arab-independence position (1915-18) conflicted with Arslan's loyalty to the Turkish-Arab union.
